core: Adverbs as modifiers of verbs, adjectives, and other adverbs
The five main adverb types: manner, time, place, degree, frequency
Forming adverbs from adjectives with -ly and its spelling rules
Adverb placement: front, middle, and end position
supporting: Adverbs with the same form as adjectives (fast, hard, late, straight)
The verb-object boundary for adverb placement

Verb classes, tense, and aspect (sibling topic)
Adverb clauses and full syntactic analysis

claims.claim: An adverb is a word that modifies a verb, an adjective, or another adverb; many adverbs are formed by adding -ly to an adjective.
Learner grammars commonly group adverbs into types by the question they answer: manner (how), time (when), place (where), degree (to what extent), and frequency (how often).

Manner adverbs are often formed from adjectives by adding -ly, with spelling adjustments: adjectives ending in -l double the l (careful becomes carefully), adjectives ending in -y change y to i (easy becomes easily), and adjectives ending in a consonant plus e keep the e (definite becomes definitely).

A small group of adverbs has the same form as the adjective (fast, hard, late, straight, well), while adjectives that already end in -ly, such as friendly, do not take a -ly adverb form and are reworded instead.
Adverbs can appear at the front, middle, or end of a clause; the mid position is between the subject and the main verb, or after the first auxiliary verb when the sentence has more than one verb.
Frequency adverbs usually go in mid position: before the main verb but after the verb be, and always, ever, and never do not usually begin a sentence.
Manner, place, and time adverbs usually go in end position, and an adverb is not placed between a verb and its object.
Degree adverbs such as very, really, and quite act as intensifiers, modifying adjectives or other adverbs, and usually appear in mid position.

Short adverbs form comparatives with -er and superlatives with -est (fast, faster, fastest), while adverbs of two or more syllables use more and most (more carefully, most carefully); combining more with an -er form is not standard.
Good is an adjective and well is its adverb, so 'I did well on the test' is standard while 'I did good' is a classic adjective-adverb confusion; well also functions as an adjective meaning healthy.
The adverb well has the irregular comparative and superlative forms better and best, and badly has worse and worst.
The adverb hardly means only just or almost not, distinct from the adverb hard, which expresses effort.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether frequency adverbs form their own type or belong under time adverbs.
positions: Cambridge Grammar's position guide gives frequency adverbs their own row with dedicated placement rules (mid position, after be).
The same source's types page discusses time adverbs without a separate frequency heading.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches manner, time, place, degree, and frequency as the five commonly used types and notes that classification lists vary by grammar.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Which adverbs take -er and -est versus more and most.
positions: Cambridge Grammar: short adverbs such as fast, hard, and early take -er and -est, while adverbs of two or more syllables take more and most.
Some learner materials generalize that adverbs are compared only with more and most because most -ly adverbs have two or more syllables.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches both systems with the no-mixing rule (more faster is not standard), which both consulted sources support.

sourceRecords.notes: Tier A per the subject source-map. Read live (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-21. Supports the core rule that adjectives modify nouns while adverbs modify verbs, adjectives, and other adverbs; -ly formation; the good/well distinction ('I did well on my exam' as the standard form, with well also meaning healthy); and degree modifiers such as really. Facts only; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Adverbs and adverb phrases: position — Cambridge Dictionary Grammar
sourceRecords.notes: Read live (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-21. Supports front/middle/end placement; mid position between subject and main verb and after the first auxiliary; the rule that adverbs come after the main verb be; frequency adverbs in mid position with always/ever/never rarely at the front; manner, place, and time adverbs in end position; degree adverbs (really, very, quite) in mid position; and the warning against placing an adverb between a verb and its object. Facts only.

sourceRecords.title: Comparison: adverbs (worse, more easily) — Cambridge Dictionary Grammar
sourceRecords.notes: Read live (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-21. Supports -er/-est for short adverbs (soon, fast, hard, early), more/most for adverbs of two or more syllables, the warning against combining more or most with an -er/-est ending, the irregular well-to-better/best and badly-to-worse/worst forms, and than to introduce the second item in a comparison. Facts only.

sourceRecords.title: Adverbs: forms — Cambridge Dictionary Grammar
sourceRecords.notes: Read live (HTTP 200) on 2026-08-21. Supports the adjective-plus-ly formation, the double-l rule (beautiful to beautifully, careful to carefully), the y-to-i rule (easy to easily, angry to angrily), keeping the e after a consonant plus e (definite to definitely, extreme to extremely), the absence of -ly forms from adjectives ending in -ly (friendly, lively), and adverbs with the same form as adjectives (fast, hard, late, straight, well). Facts only.
